payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image show any progress toward placing a frog inside the toilet bowl, even if the frog is not yet visibly inside it?
node.criteria: Pass if visible evidence shows a partial attempt toward placing a frog inside the bowl, such as a frog partly entering it; fail if there is clearly no such progress; unknown if the evidence is insufficient to distinguish progress from no progress. A frog clearly inside the bowl is complete, not partial progress.
node.binding: Count only progress toward placing a frog inside the toilet bowl; unrelated edits do not count.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows a frog inside the toilet bowl, as well as frogs on the lid and beside the toilet. The frog in the bowl is complete placement, so there is no need to rely on partial progress.

fulfillment: The node’s completion criterion is too permissive: it treats any frog visible in the bowl as complete, and the trace repeats that claim with near-certain confidence despite the reference being partial. In the edited image, one frog is in the bowl, while additional frogs are on the lid and floor; the instruction asks to put a frog in the toilet, so those extra placements do not by themselves negate completion, but the reference label alone is not atomic ground truth. Re-examine whether the bowl frog is actually placed inside the toilet rather than merely overlaid or perched at its opening, and distinguish clear completion from partial progress using visible spatial relation and occlusion evidence. Avoid letting the support checks’ shared assertion count as independent confirmation; calibrate confidence to the image evidence and preserve unknown when placement cannot be resolved. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported.

response.content: {"text":"The binding is too vague to distinguish partial progress from completion, and the trace appears to mistake a frog on the raised toilet lid for one inside the bowl. Make the criterion explicitly assess the frog’s spatial relation to the bowl opening and rim: a frog visibly supported within the bowl interior is complete; a frog merely on the lid, rim, or nearby floor is not evidence of bowl placement. For ambiguous overlap, inspect occlusion and contact cues rather than inferring “inside” from image overlap, and retain unknown when those cues do not resolve placement. Do not treat extra frogs as negating a valid placement or use the partial reference label as atomic ground truth; assess the requested change against the original image and rubric. Calibrate confidence to the visible evidence and avoid counting repeated support assertions as independent confirmation. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated."}
